title: Hold Fire
mood: A gray shape climbs the tower toward the console, and Lesley has to wait for Chang’e’s word.

hero.alt: Official art: Lesley, blonde hair tied high, stands on a steel girder high above a city with her long orange rifle resting on her shoulder.

segs.t: Lesley stood where she had stood all day, behind Chang’e’s chair, one hand on its back. Down the side of the console the thin lines were still climbing, one for every suit in the city.
Through the top of the long window there was no sky left. The Storm Citadel hung over the Academy, close enough to count its towers.
The second front,
thought Lesley.
Here.
Then the floor began to hum.
It came up through her boots. The glass in the long window buzzed in its frame. Mr. Bunny’s ears went flat.
Lesley swung the rifle off her shoulder.
The light woke under the ship, over the hall’s roofs, and the tower was already inside it. The whole deck went magenta.
On the rifle, the coil Chang’e had built went cold in her hands.
It had run cooler than the old one since the dawn she fitted it. Now it lay along the barrel, dead metal.
Around Chang’e’s chair the small crescents dropped out of the air. They rang on the floor and lay still.
Chang’e looked down at them. She did not pick them up.
The console stayed lit, and so did the channel’s green light. Mr. Bunny still hung at her shoulder with his screen on.
Lesley’s machine eye still drew the deck in thin teal lines. Chang’e had built it at the old base, before there were any suits. Nothing in it ran on aspirant power.
She drew the bolt back by hand, to see if it still worked.
Under the dead coil the old action slid back and locked home. Clack.
The day Chang’e gave her this rifle, she had thought,
It’ll still work in the dark.

Through the window she watched the edge of the light roll on down the hill toward the water. On the console the thin lines fell flat in the order it reached them. The last to go was a speck of gold, flying in fast from over the water. It dropped out of the air at the mouth of the bay road cut, and the last line lay flat.
Chang’e’s hands had stopped on the keys.
Lesley keyed the channel and told the frontline what the board showed. Then she gave the next order.
“Frontline. Pull back into the bay road cut. One street. Hold it.”

A line with no power, spread over a district, was a dead line. In one narrow street, with the shelters at its back, people on foot could hold. She had held streets like that for the Shield, before there were any suits. Guinevere already lay at the cut’s mouth.
“Rear support behind them, with the wounded.”
Chang’e was still looking at the crescents on the floor.
“Big Sis said imagination is my weapon.”
She said it to the console. Lesley had said it once, to a room of Shield officers, with Chang’e on a crate beside her. She had not known Chang’e kept it.

media.alt: Official art: young Chang'e, with glasses and big headphones, and Lesley stand back to back in warm light, each looking away in profile.
media.credit: Official Lesley and Chang'e art, Renewed Hope

segs.t: Chang’e’s hands went back to the keys. She laid the new hum over the ship’s outline on her screen.
“It isn’t the storm,” she said. “It’s coming from the middle of the ship. From one long thing that runs through it. Every block hangs off it.”
“A mast?”
“It reads alive. Like an Ender’s insides.” She frowned at the screen. “Like a spine.”
“Can we hit it?”
“Not from here. Not with anything we have.”
Lesley looked down at the rifle. A spring, a pin and a bolt, and plain rounds. A plain round rang off Ender plate. It went only into an open core.
Outside, below the sill, claws scraped on stone.
Her machine eye found it first. At the bottom edge of the glass, teal lines came up the tower’s face hand over hand, straight toward the console.
The glass burst inward. Rain blew across the keys. A gray arm hooked over the frame, then a head and shoulders, and an Ender hauled itself half into the deck.
It was three times Chang’e’s height. Its chest was plated shut.
It bent toward the small girl at the console, and it did not strike. They never struck easily.
Lesley’s rifle was already up. Against shut plate it was no use.
Her feet had started round the chair.
Then I’ll stand in front.
She had said it every night to her little brother, who held her sleeve.
“Stay at my back, Big Sis,” said Chang’e. She had not turned her head. “That worked last time.”
Lesley stopped.
“It won’t open till it strikes,” said Chang’e. “I hold still. It strikes at me. The core opens. You fire.”
“Get down.”
“Then it strikes when it likes, where you can’t see. And the street goes blind.” Chang’e’s hands lay flat on the console. “Mr. Bunny takes the hit. You take the shot.”
Lesley had seen the plan before Chang’e finished saying it. There was no better one on the deck.
The old answer was already in her mouth.
No.
She had given it every time Chang’e asked for a place on the rotation.
Chang’e spoke first.
“I can’t keep hiding in Big Sis’s shadow. I’ll fight and grow, too.”
Lesley’s voice came out rough. “Don’t make me do this. Chang’e...”
Chang’e did not move. Mr. Bunny hung very still at her shoulder.
Lesley had given her reason only once.
In the field, I can’t see you.
Now the fight had come to the deck. There were no roofs between them here, and no water. Chang’e sat one step in front of her, in the light of her own console, close enough to touch.
I can see her,
she thought.
And she’s asking me.
She rested the barrel on the back of Chang’e’s chair, where her hand had been, the muzzle out over Chang’e’s head. She set her cheek to the stock.
“On your call.”
“Don’t fire early, Big Sis,” said Chang’e. “Wait till it’s wide. I’ll call it.”
Chang’e folded her hands on the console and held still. Rain ran down her glasses. She did not wipe them.
The Ender’s arm went up.
Its chest plates began to part. In Lesley’s eye the gap was one teal line, then a sliver. A round in a sliver would hit the edge of the plate.
The claw came down at Chang’e’s head.
Every year of Lesley’s life told her finger to fire. The sliver widened. Chang’e sat under the falling claw with her hands folded.
Not yet. She said she’d call it.
Lesley held. One heartbeat.
“Front,” said Chang’e.
Mr. Bunny swung in front of her face. The claw struck his casing with a crack and sent him spinning down the console.
The plates stood wide. The core burned inside them.
Lesley fired over Chang’e’s head.
The old action kicked into her shoulder. Her round went into the open core, and the core went dark. The Ender slid back off the sill and fell away down the tower.
The empty frame let in the wind.

Mr. Bunny bounced off the end of the console and caught himself in the air. One ear hung crooked. A dent ran across his casing where the claw had hit. His screen flickered, then found its smile with the eyes shut, and he floated back to Chang’e’s shoulder.
Lesley’s finger stayed on the trigger a long moment after there was nothing left to shoot.
She came round the chair and stopped a step away, the way she always stopped.
Chang’e had pulled Mr. Bunny into her lap. Her glasses sat crooked.
Then Lesley did not stop. She knelt among the dead crescents, level with the chair, and put her arms around Chang’e and the dented robot both.
Chang’e’s hands stayed on Mr. Bunny. She did not push her away.
Lesley had carried the words since the night of the crater. Once she had thought them in a tower window across the water, with the rifle in her hands. She had never said them aloud.
She said them now, low, against the top of Chang’e’s head.
“Ever since that day, I vowed to keep you safe, Chang’e.”
Rain ticked on the console.
“I know,” said Chang’e. It came out small. “Mr. Bunny showed me. A roof and a rifle, that night, and the next, and the next. I told him to turn around.”
She swallowed.
“I looked anyway.”
On the avenue, the night the Enders came back, the girl on the stones had turned around and looked straight up at Lesley’s window. She had not searched the shore for it. She had known which one.
Lesley’s arms tightened. Mr. Bunny’s bent ear pressed against her collar.

media.alt: Lesley stands in a high window at night, her long rifle across her body, the moon over the city behind the glass.

segs.t: “Deck,” said Fanny on the channel. “They’re nearly at the cut.”
Lesley let go and stood. Chang’e set her glasses straight and turned back to the console.
Lesley keyed the open channel, to every Aspirant in the city whose suit had gone dark.
“As long as we have heart, we will never surrender.”
On Chang’e’s console the light for mobile support was still blinking.
Through the broken window Lesley’s eye caught the Academy’s bell tower, small under the ship. Lightning was crawling over its roof. Nothing on the console named it.
Then the lightning climbed the wrong way, up off the tiles.
